chapter_theme: Knowing strength: the deed's, one's own, the opponent's and the allies', and treating wealth as a form of strength with a limit. The theme is limits, and most of the chapter warns against zeal, generosity and pride that outrun them.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar's divisions: the parts of strength and the reward for knowing them (471-472), the cost of not knowing one's own (473-474), the opponent's and allies' (475), the deed's (476), and wealth as a part of strength (477-480).

471.reading: Weigh the strength of the deed, one's own strength, the opponent's strength and the strength of allies, and then act.
471.nuance: The first item is surprising: the deed itself has strength. Parimelazhagar adds a strict rule the verse doesn't state, that one should act only if one's own side is greater, and avoid even an equal contest, since victory there is doubtful.

472.reading: For those who know what they can do and what must be known, and proceed resting in that, nothing fails.
472.nuance: The chapter's only verse of confidence, and it hangs on அதன்கண் தங்கி, where the commentators pull in nearly opposite directions.

positions.position: Resting means total commitment: fixing mind, speech and body on the task while marching.
positions.quote: எப்பொழுதும் மன, மொழி, மெய்களை அதன் கண் வைத்துப் பகைமேல் செல்லும் அரசர்க்கு;

positions.position: Resting means restraint: staying within the measure of what one knows one can do.

473.reading: Many, not knowing the strength they have, rose on enthusiasm and were broken midway.
473.nuance: A rare verse appealing to history, பலர். ஊக்கத்தின் ஊக்கி uses the very quality demanded of kings in 382 as the cause of the fall. Not knowing runs both ways too, as உடைத்தம் வலி means the strength they do have.

474.reading: One who doesn't live in accord, doesn't know his measure and admires himself perishes quickly.
474.nuance: Parimelazhagar makes ஆங்கு அமைந்து about neighbouring kings: one must be either a friend or an enemy who knows his strength. Others read it as a general composure, or as respect for people.

475.reading: Even a cart loaded with peacock feathers breaks its axle, if that load is piled too high.
475.nuance: The two உம் make both the cart strong and the load light. The verse speaks only of the cart, and the allegory is supplied by the commentators.

positions.position: The feathers are weak enemies: even the strong fail when many combine against them.
positions.quote: 'எளியர்' என்று பலரோடு பகைகொள்வான். தான் வலியனே ஆயினும் அவர் தொக்க வழி வலியழியும்;

positions.position: The cart is a fortress: those who trust in strong forts learn that defences fail if the enemy grows too much.
positions.quote: இஃது அரண் மிகுதல் நன் றென்றிருப்பார்க்குப் பகைமிகின் அரண் நில்லா தென்று கூறிற்று.

476.reading: Those who have climbed to the tip of a branch and strive further will end their life.
476.nuance: The climber has done well to get there, and that is the danger: this is a warning to the successful. The verse is purely image. Parimelazhagar applies it to a king who has gone as far as he can on a campaign, and Manakkudavar has him turn back.

477.reading: Give in the proper way, knowing the measure; that is the way of guarding wealth and bestowing it.
477.nuance: The verse fuses the two usually opposed, போற்றி and வழங்கு, into one way. Parimelazhagar's fixed ratio, two parts for spending, one for reserves and one for giving, comes from Tirikadugam, not the verse.

478.reading: Though the channel of income be narrow, there is no ruin, if the channel of outgo isn't wider.
478.nuance: ஆறு is a path or channel, which gives wealth a hydraulic image. Income's size doesn't determine ruin; only the ratio does. Parimelazhagar adds that even exact balance is safe.

479.reading: The life of one who doesn't live knowing the measure seems to exist, then is not, and perishes without a trace.
479.nuance: The verse has three stages: seeming, not being and not even seeming. Parimelazhagar points out that ruin isn't visible at the start, which is why the first stage is a seeming and the warning needed.

480.reading: Helpfulness that doesn't weigh the limit of what one has quickly ends the limit of one's wealth.
480.nuance: Even the most praised social virtue gets a limit. Manakkudavar sees the objection coming: if spending must stay below income, how can one be helpful? This is presented as the answer.

links.note: 220 says if helpfulness brings ruin, it is worth buying even by selling oneself. 480 says helpfulness that ignores one's means quickly destroys wealth. Aram and Porul give opposite counsel on the same act, and 480 uses the same word, ஒப்புரவு.

595 says a person's height rises with their spirit, as a lotus stem with the water. 473 says many have been broken by exactly that spirit, ஊக்கம், when it wasn't measured. One counts spirit as the measure and the other demands a measure for spirit.
Prosperity that perishes while appearing to exist or grow. 283 blames fraud and 479 blames not knowing the measure, so honest wealth and stolen wealth can fail in the same deceptive way.
385 ends the royal wealth cycle in distribution. 477 sets the limit on that distribution. Parimelazhagar explicitly connects them, sending the reader back to 385 for the way of giving.

source_issues: 475: Kalaignar's comment says the cart gets so strong that the axle breaks, which appears garbled and doesn't fit the verse. I did not use it.
